questions.question: Why is <button onclick="..."> preferred over <div onclick="..."> for a clickable control?
options: div elements cannot have onclick handlers at all
button is automatically keyboard-focusable, announced as a button by screen readers, and already responds to Enter/Space — a div needs tabindex, role, and keydown handlers added manually to match
button elements render faster in the browser
There is no actual accessibility difference between the two
questions.explanation: Native interactive elements come with keyboard focusability, correct semantics, and key handling built in; replicating that on a div requires several additional manual steps.

questions.question: What is the 'first rule of ARIA' referenced in the lesson?
options: Always add as many ARIA attributes as possible to be safe
Don't use ARIA if a native HTML element or attribute already provides the semantics and behavior you need
ARIA should only be used on form elements
ARIA attributes must always be paired with a role attribute
questions.explanation: Native HTML elements provide correct accessibility semantics for free; ARIA is for the gap where no native element covers the pattern you need (like a custom tab panel).

questions.question: What does `aria-hidden="true"` do?
options: Visually hides the element from sighted users
Removes the element from the accessibility tree so assistive technology skips it entirely, appropriate for purely decorative content
Disables the element so it cannot be clicked
Makes the element load lazily for performance
questions.explanation: aria-hidden only affects the accessibility tree, not visual rendering — it's used to prevent decorative icons/emoji from being announced redundantly.

questions.question: Why is <button role="link">Submit</button> considered harmful rather than just redundant?
options: It will cause the button to stop working entirely
It overrides the button's implicit role with a contradictory one, so assistive tech announces it as a link while it still behaves like a button — a mismatch ARIA is supposed to prevent, not cause
role attributes are deprecated in HTML5
It has no effect either way since browsers ignore conflicting roles
questions.explanation: Overriding a native element's role to something that contradicts its actual behavior actively misleads assistive technology users about how the control works.
